The story

The brand's story began in 1854 as the Waterbury Clock Company in Waterbury, Connecticut, which initially mass-produced affordable clocks and later, in partnership with Ingersoll, the famous "dollar" pocket watch. During World War I, the company adapted pocket watches for the wrist, and during World War II, as the U.S. Time Corporation, it produced military timers. After the war, the company focused on wristwatches, introducing the Timex brand in 1950 with the durable V-Conic movement. Through the 1950s and '60s, Timex became a household name with its famous "It takes a licking and keeps on ticking" television torture tests and its popular mechanical models like the dressy Marlin and the automatic Viscount. The quartz crisis of the 1970s was a turning point; the company embraced the new technology, launching its first quartz watch in 1972 and branding these models with a "Q," as seen in the now-reissued Q Timex designs. This era was followed by the creation of the military-inspired MK1 Mechanical, based on a 1982 disposable watch. The brand's reputation for innovation continued with the launch of the iconic Ironman sports watch in 1986 and the revolutionary Indiglo night-light in 1992. The popular Weekender line, known for its strap versatility, has been a canvas for many collaborations, including with Peanuts. Today, Timex continues to produce a wide range of accessible quartz and mechanical watches, often drawing on its extensive archive. The Waterbury collection, including the Waterbury Classic and the pilot-style Waterbury Ace Fly-Back Chronograph, pays homage to the company's origins. The Expedition line, introduced in the mid-1990s, offers rugged outdoor models like the Expedition Scout, with the more recent Expedition North sub-collection featuring premium models like the Expedition North Titanium Automatic and the function-driven Expedition North Tide-Temp-Compass. The brand's Legacy collection continues to offer timeless, classic designs.
